title: Google Search Central, SEO Starter Guide
text:
## Core principle
Google uses automated crawlers to discover web pages. Most sites are found naturally without extra work; following Google's Search Essentials makes a site more eligible to appear, and SEO is the further work to improve search presence. Changes take time: some effects show in hours, others in months, so wait a few weeks before assessing whether work helped.

## Help Google find your content
Use the site: search operator (for example site:wikipedia.org) to verify content is indexed. Google primarily finds pages through links from already-crawled pages; other sites linking to yours happens naturally over time. You may submit a sitemap but it is not required. Google needs to access the same resources as the user's browser: if a site blocks CSS and JavaScript, Google may not understand or rank the pages well. Use Search Console's URL Inspection Tool to see how Google renders a page.

## Organize your site with descriptive URLs
Parts of the URL can be shown as breadcrumbs in results, so URLs help users judge whether a result is useful. A good URL like https://www.example.com/pets/cats.html beats an opaque one like https://www.example.com/2/6772756D707920636174. Group similar content into directories; Google learns how often each directory updates and adjusts crawl frequency. Duplicate content across many URLs wastes crawling; use rel=canonical or redirects, though Google tries to canonicalize automatically.

## Make your site interesting and useful
Content should be easy to read and well organized, unique (do not copy others), up to date, and helpful, reliable, and people-first. Anticipate search intent: experts and novices use different keywords. Minimize distracting ads and interstitials. Link strategically with descriptive anchor text so users and engines understand a linked page before visiting. Add nofollow to user-generated links to avoid associating your site with untrusted resources.

## Influence your appearance in Search
The title link comes from the page's <title> element: make it unique to the page, clear, concise, and accurate. Snippets are drawn from page content; the meta description tag can also source them, so keep it short, unique to the page, and covering the most relevant points. For images, use sharp images placed near relevant text and write short descriptive alt text explaining the image's relationship to the content. For video, embed high-quality video on a standalone page near relevant text.

## What NOT to focus on (myth-busting from Google)
Google Search does not use the keywords meta tag. Keyword stuffing (excessively repeating words, even in variations) is against spam policies. Keywords in the domain or URL path have hardly any effect beyond breadcrumbs. The TLD (.com, .org) usually matters only for country targeting and is a low-impact signal. There is no magical word count, minimum or maximum, and length alone does not affect ranking. Subdomains vs subdirectories: do whatever makes business sense. Duplicate content across your own URLs is inefficient but does not trigger a manual action or penalty (copying others' content is different and prohibited). Heading semantic order matters for screen readers, not for ranking, and there is no ideal number of headings. On E-E-A-T: it is not itself a direct ranking factor.

title: Google Search Central, In-Depth Guide to How Google Search Works
text:
## Three stages
Google Search works in three stages, and not all pages make it through each one: crawling, indexing, and serving search results.

## Crawling
Google finds URLs by revisiting known pages, following links from known pages, and reading submitted sitemaps. There is no central registry of all web pages, so Google must constantly look for new and updated pages. The crawler is called Googlebot; it uses an algorithmic process to determine which sites to crawl, how often, and how many pages to fetch from each site, and it rate-limits to avoid overloading servers. During crawling Google renders the page and runs any JavaScript using a recent version of Chrome, because sites often rely on JavaScript to bring content to the page. Common reasons Googlebot cannot crawl: server errors, network issues, and robots.txt rules.

## Indexing
After a page is crawled, Google tries to understand what it is about, processing textual content and key content tags and attributes such as <title> elements and alt attributes, plus images and videos. During indexing Google determines whether a page is a duplicate of another or canonical: it groups pages with similar content into a cluster and selects the one most representative of the group as the canonical, which is shown in results. Other pages in the cluster are alternate versions served in different contexts, for example when a user searches on mobile. Google also collects signals about the canonical page and its content, such as language, country the content is local to, and usability. Being crawled does not guarantee indexing.

## Serving search results
When a user searches, Google returns the highest-quality, most relevant results, considering hundreds of factors including the user's location, language, and device. Ranking is done programmatically and Google does not accept payment to rank pages higher. Search features shown depend on the query: a local business query may show a local map, a shopping query may show images. An indexed page may still not appear if its content is low quality, if robots meta rules prevent serving, or if it does not match what users are searching for.

title: Google Search Central, Introduction to robots.txt
text:
## What robots.txt is
A robots.txt file tells search engine crawlers which URLs the crawler can access on your site. It is used mainly to avoid overloading a site with requests; it is not a mechanism for keeping a web page out of Google.

## Crawling vs indexing (the critical distinction)
Blocking a URL in robots.txt controls crawling, not indexing. A page that is disallowed in robots.txt can still be indexed if it is linked to from other pages or sites. When that happens, Google may show the URL in results without a description, because it was not allowed to fetch the content. To actually keep a page out of the index, do not rely on robots.txt; use a noindex meta tag or response header, or password protection.

## Limitations
Robots.txt rules are not supported by all search engines and different crawlers interpret the syntax differently. Robots.txt is not a security mechanism: it will not stop misbehaving or malicious crawlers, and disallowed content can still be discovered and indexed through external links. For media and resource files, robots.txt can manage crawl traffic, but for reliably preventing a page from appearing in search you must use noindex rather than a Disallow rule (and note that if a page is blocked by robots.txt, Google cannot see the noindex directive on it).

title: Google Search Central, Learn about sitemaps
text:
## What a sitemap is
A sitemap is a file that lists the pages, videos, and other files on your site and their relationships. Google reads a sitemap to crawl a site more efficiently and to learn which content you consider important. A sitemap can also carry specialized metadata: for video (running time, rating, age-appropriateness), for images (their location on your pages), and for news (article title and publication date).

## When you need one
A sitemap helps if the site is large (more than 500 pages), if the site is new and has few external links pointing to it, or if it has rich media (video, images) or news content you want surfaced. It is less necessary when the site is small (around 500 pages or fewer), when Googlebot can find all important pages by following links from the home page, or when there is little media or news content.

## Important limitation
A sitemap helps search engines discover URLs on your site, but it does not guarantee that all items in the sitemap will be crawled and indexed. Many content management systems (WordPress, Wix, Blogger) generate a sitemap automatically.

title: Google Search Central, How to specify a canonical URL with rel=canonical and other methods
text:
## What a canonical URL is
When several URLs carry identical or substantially similar content, the canonical URL is the preferred version. If you do not specify one, Google identifies which version is objectively the best to show users in Search.

## Why canonicalization matters
Specifying a canonical lets you control which URL appears in results, consolidates ranking signals (such as links to the individual URLs) into a single preferred URL, simplifies analytics for one piece of content, and helps Googlebot spend crawl effort on new or updated content rather than duplicates.

## Methods, ranked by strength
Redirects are a strong signal that the redirect target should be canonical; use permanent (301) redirects when retiring a duplicate. A rel=canonical link element in the HTML head is a strong signal: use absolute URLs, include a self-referential canonical on the canonical page itself, and keep it in the head only. A rel=canonical HTTP header is the equivalent for non-HTML files like PDFs (Link: <https://www.example.com/downloads/white-paper.pdf>; rel="canonical"). Including a URL in a sitemap is a weak signal. Google also prefers HTTPS over HTTP and prefers URLs that are part of an hreflang cluster.

## What NOT to do
Do not use robots.txt for canonicalization: Google may still index a disallowed URL without its content. Do not use the URL removal tool for canonicalization, because it hides all versions of a URL from Search. Do not point conflicting canonicals with different methods. Do not use URL fragments as canonicals. Do not use noindex to consolidate duplicates, because it blocks the page from Search entirely. Link consistently to your canonical URLs across the site.

title: Google Search Central, Creating helpful, reliable, people-first content
text:
## Self-assessment: content and quality
Google recommends judging your own content by whether it provides original information, reporting, research, or analysis; whether it gives a substantial, complete, or comprehensive description of the topic; whether it avoids simply rewriting other sources; whether it is accurate; and whether it is polished rather than hastily produced. Ask whether the content provides insightful analysis or interesting information beyond the obvious.

## People-first vs search-engine-first content
People-first content is made primarily to help people and serves an existing or intended audience who would find it useful if they came to you directly. It should demonstrate first-hand expertise and depth of knowledge. Search-engine-first content shows warning signs: producing lots of content hoping some ranks, relying mainly on automation, mostly summarizing what others say without adding value, writing to a word count because you heard Google prefers it, chasing a trending topic you do not normally cover, or changing the date of pages to make them seem fresh when the content has not substantially changed.

## The Who, How, and Why framework
Who: make clear who authored the content, with bylines and author background. How: be transparent about how the content was produced, especially any automation or AI generation, and explain why automation was a good approach. Why: content should exist primarily to help people, not primarily to attract search traffic and manipulate rankings.

## E-E-A-T and YMYL
Google's systems reward content that shows Experience, Expertise, Authoritativeness, and Trustworthiness (E-E-A-T), and of these Trust is the most important; the others contribute to trust. Experience (was the content produced with some degree of first-hand or life experience) was added to the earlier E-A-T. E-E-A-T matters most for Your Money or Your Life (YMYL) topics that could affect health, financial stability, safety, or wellbeing.

title: Google Search Central, Spam policies for Google web search
text:
## Cloaking
Showing different content to users than to search engines to manipulate rankings, for example showing a page about travel to Google while showing discount drugs to users, or injecting keywords only when the requester is a search engine.

## Doorways
Sites or pages created to rank for specific, similar queries that then funnel users to one intermediate destination, including many near-duplicate pages targeting regions or cities.

## Expired domain abuse
Buying an expired domain and repurposing it mainly to manipulate rankings with content of little user value, for example affiliate content on a domain formerly used by a government agency.

## Hacked content, hidden text and links
Content placed via security vulnerabilities (code, page, or content injection, malicious redirects). Hidden text and links means content placed only to manipulate engines and not seen by users: white text on white background, text behind an image, off-screen CSS, font size or opacity zero, single-character links.

## Keyword stuffing
Filling a page with keywords or numbers unnaturally, for example lists of phone numbers with no added value, blocks of text listing cities and regions, or the same words and phrases repeated so often it sounds unnatural.

## Link spam
Links created mainly to manipulate rankings: buying or selling links (or exchanging goods/services or products for links), excessive link exchanges, automated link building, requiring a link as part of terms of service, text advertisements or advertorials without qualifying the links (nofollow/sponsored), and keyword-rich hidden links in widgets or footers distributed across sites.

## Machine-generated traffic and malicious behavior
Sending automated queries to Google (for example scraping rankings) consumes resources and violates policy. Malware and malicious behavior, unwanted software, and misleading functionality (like a fake generator claiming to provide something it never delivers) are all violations.

## Scaled content abuse
Generating many pages mainly to manipulate rankings and not help users, whether by automation, human effort, or a combination. Examples include using generative AI to produce many pages without adding value, stitching or combining content from different pages without adding value, and creating pages where the content makes little sense but contains search keywords. The focus is on scaled production to manipulate rankings, regardless of how it is produced.

## Scraped content, sneaky redirects, thin affiliate
Republishing others' content (copied verbatim, lightly modified, or compiled) without adding value. Sneaky redirects send users somewhere different from what Google saw. Thin affiliate pages carry copied product descriptions with no original value, often cookie-cutter templates repeated across domains.

## Site reputation abuse
Publishing third-party pages on a reputable host site mainly to exploit the host's ranking signals with little host oversight, for example a payday-loan or casino review section placed on an education or medical domain.

## User-generated spam
Spam added by users through channels like forum posts, comment sections, or file uploads, often without the site owner's knowledge.

title: Google Search Central, Introduction to structured data markup
text:
## What structured data is
Structured data is a standardized format for providing information about a page and classifying the page content, so search engines can understand the page's meaning through explicit markup. Google uses it to understand content and to enable rich results: more visually engaging listings with extra features that can increase engagement.

## Formats
Three formats are supported. JSON-LD is recommended: JavaScript object notation embedded in a script tag in the head or body, easiest to implement and maintain at scale. Microdata uses HTML tag attributes to nest structured data within content. RDFa is an HTML5 extension using tag attributes. Most structured data for Search uses the schema.org vocabulary, but Google's documentation is the authority for Search-specific behavior.

## Guidelines (content quality)
Structured data must represent content that is visible to users. Do not mark up content that is not visible to readers, do not create blank or empty pages just to hold structured data, and do not add markup for false, misleading, or irrelevant information. The markup should be representative of the main content of the page, relevant, complete, and not misleading. Use the Rich Results Test to validate markup before deployment; eligibility for rich results is not guaranteed by valid markup alone.

title: Google Search Central, Understanding page experience in Google Search results
text:
## What page experience means
Google's core ranking systems look to reward content that provides a good page experience. There is no single page experience signal or ranking metric; the systems look at a variety of signals that align with overall page experience. Relevance stays paramount: strong page experience helps decide among many relevant results, but does not override relevance.

## Self-assessment checklist
Google offers questions site owners can ask themselves: Do your pages have good Core Web Vitals? Are your pages served over HTTPS in a secure fashion? Does content display well on mobile devices? Does the content avoid an excessive number of ads that distract from or interfere with the main content? Do your pages avoid using intrusive interstitials? Is your page designed so visitors can easily distinguish the main content from other content?

## Guidance
Rather than chasing a single number, focus on delivering overall great page experience across these dimensions. Good page experience combined with helpful, reliable, people-first content is the goal; the Core Web Vitals metrics and their thresholds are documented separately in the Core Web Vitals guidance.

title: web.dev (Google), Web Vitals
text:
## Definition
Web Vitals is an initiative by Google to provide unified guidance for quality signals essential to delivering a great user experience on the web. Core Web Vitals are the subset that apply to all pages, are measurable in the field, and reflect real user-centered outcomes.

## The three Core Web Vitals and their good thresholds
Largest Contentful Paint (LCP) measures loading performance: LCP should occur within 2.5 seconds of when the page first starts loading. Interaction to Next Paint (INP) measures interactivity: pages should have an INP of 200 milliseconds or less. Cumulative Layout Shift (CLS) measures visual stability: pages should maintain a CLS of 0.1 or less.

## Measurement
To ensure you hit the target for most users, measure the 75th percentile of page loads, segmented across mobile and desktop devices. A page passes when it meets all three thresholds at the 75th percentile.

## Supporting and diagnostic metrics
Time to First Byte (TTFB) and First Contentful Paint (FCP) are diagnostic metrics that help identify loading problems. Total Blocking Time (TBT) is a lab proxy for INP because real user interaction cannot be measured in a simulated lab environment. Lab measurement is best during development, while field data captures real device and network conditions that the lab cannot replicate.

title: Google Search Central, Mobile-first indexing best practices
text:
## What mobile-first indexing is
Google predominantly uses the mobile version of a site's content, crawled with the smartphone Googlebot, for indexing and ranking. All new sites are indexed mobile-first.

## Site configurations
Responsive design (recommended) serves the same HTML on one URL and adapts by screen size. Dynamic serving returns different HTML at the same URL based on user-agent. Separate URLs serve different HTML and URLs per device.

## Content parity is the core rule
Make sure the mobile site contains the same content as the desktop site. If the mobile version has less, consider accordions or tabs rather than removing content. Title elements and meta descriptions should be equivalent on both versions. Use the same structured data on both, and prioritize markup like Breadcrumb, Product, and VideoObject. Images and videos should use the same alt text, supported formats, stable URLs, and accessible placement; do not lazy-load primary content in a way that hides it.

## Common mistakes
Applying noindex on the mobile version, blocking resources with robots.txt, missing or mismatched structured data or metadata between versions, low-quality or blocked images, using URL fragments to load content, serving error pages on mobile, redirecting several desktop pages to a single mobile URL, and having insufficient server capacity for the smartphone crawl rate.

title: Google Search Central, Understand the JavaScript SEO basics
text:
## The three-phase processing model
Google processes JavaScript apps in three phases: crawling, rendering, and indexing. During crawling, Googlebot fetches a URL, checks robots.txt, and parses the HTML for links. Pages that return a 200 status are queued for rendering, where a headless Chromium runs the JavaScript and produces rendered HTML. During indexing, Google uses the rendered HTML to index the content and to find more URLs to crawl.

## Deferred rendering
Rendering does not happen instantly. A page may sit on the render queue for a few seconds, though it can take longer, because Google renders when resources allow. So JavaScript-dependent content is indexed only after this delay.

## Best practices
Use unique, descriptive title elements and meta descriptions; you can set them with JavaScript. Set the canonical URL correctly (JavaScript can inject a rel=canonical, but keep it consistent). Use meaningful HTTP status codes, for example a real 404 for a missing page. In single-page apps avoid soft 404s: either redirect to a server-rendered 404 URL or add a noindex robots meta tag via JavaScript on the error state. Use the History API for routing between views rather than URL fragments, because fragments prevent Googlebot from discovering distinct URLs. Do not block JavaScript resources in robots.txt, since that blocks rendering entirely. Implement lazy-loading so images still load in a search-friendly way, and verify web component (shadow DOM) content appears in the rendered HTML.

title: Google Search Central, Large site owner's guide to managing crawl budget
text:
## Definition
Crawl budget is the set of URLs that Google can and wants to crawl, formed by combining crawl capacity limit and crawl demand. Budget is per host (example.com and code.example.com have separate budgets).

## Who needs to worry about it
Most sites do not. This matters for large sites with more than 1 million unique pages that change about weekly, and medium or larger sites with more than 10,000 unique pages that change daily, and sites with a large share of URLs shown as Discovered, currently not indexed in Search Console.

## The two components
Crawl capacity limit (crawl rate) is how much crawling a site can handle without being overwhelmed: it goes up when the site responds quickly and reliably and goes down when the server slows, returns 5xx server errors, or responds with HTTP 429 rate limiting. Crawl demand depends on perceived inventory, URL popularity, and staleness: Google crawls popular and frequently updated URLs more.

## Best practices
Consolidate duplicate content so crawling focuses on unique content. Block crawling of low-value URLs with robots.txt (infinite scroll variants, sort-parameter duplicates). For permanently removed pages return 404 or 410 rather than blocking with robots.txt. Eliminate soft 404s, which keep consuming budget. Keep sitemaps current and use lastmod for updated URLs. Avoid long redirect chains. Improve server response time and support the 304 Not Modified status so unchanged pages are cheaper to recrawl.

title: Google Search Central, Qualify your outbound links to Google (nofollow, sponsored, ugc)
text:
## The three rel values
Use rel="sponsored" for links that are advertisements or paid placements, commonly called paid links. Use rel="ugc" for user-generated content links such as comments and forum posts; you may remove ugc from contributions by trusted, long-standing members over time. Use rel="nofollow" when the other values do not apply and you would rather Google not associate your site with, or crawl, the linked page.

## Combining and treatment
You can combine values, space or comma separated, for example rel="ugc nofollow". Links carrying these attributes will generally not be followed, though the linked pages can still be discovered and crawled through other means such as sitemaps or links elsewhere. These attributes are used as hints for crawling and indexing purposes. Historically nofollow was introduced to fight comment spam; in 2019 Google evolved nofollow and added the sponsored and ugc types, and began treating them as hints rather than strict directives. Marking paid or sponsored links (rather than passing plain followed links) keeps you clear of the link spam policy on buying and selling links.

title: Google Search Central, Influence your title links in search results
text:
## What a title link is
The title link is the clickable title of a search result that links to the page. It is often the primary piece of information users use to decide which result to click.

## How Google generates it
Google generates the title link automatically from several sources: the content of the page's <title> element, the main visual title shown on the page, heading elements such as <h1>, other large and prominent text, the og:title meta tag, anchor text pointing to the page from other sites, and WebSite structured data. The title element is the primary source.

## Best practices for the title element
Give every page a title element. Write descriptive, concise titles that reflect the page. Avoid keyword stuffing and repeating the same words. Avoid repeated or boilerplate titles across many pages; make each page's title unique. Brand your titles concisely, using a delimiter such as a colon or pipe, and do not repeat unnecessary site-name branding on every page. Match the primary language and script of the page. Make the on-page main title visually prominent so Google can identify it.

## Why Google rewrites titles
Google may replace the title link when the title element is empty, obscured, or stuffed with keywords; when it is boilerplate repeated across the site; when it is inaccurate or half-empty; when there is a language or script mismatch; or when the site name is unnecessarily duplicated. Writing clean, accurate, unique titles reduces rewrites.

title: Google Search Console Help, Performance report (Search)
text:
## The four metrics
Clicks is the number of times a user clicked through to your site from Google Search results. Impressions is how many times a URL from your site appeared in search results (a link must be scrolled into view for some result types, but generally counts when it appears on the results page). CTR (click-through rate) is clicks divided by impressions, expressed as a percentage. Average position is the average of the topmost position your site occupied for the query, so a lower number is better (position 1 is the top).

## Dimensions
You can break performance down by query (the search terms typed), page (the landing URL), country, device, search appearance (the result feature, such as a rich result), and date. This lets you see, for example, which queries drive impressions but few clicks (a title or snippet problem) versus which rank low but convert well.

## Aggregation caveats
Queries, countries, devices, and dates are aggregated at the property level; pages and search appearance aggregate by page. Because results are personalized by time, location, device, and history, a query in your report may not show your site when you search it yourself. Use position with clicks and impressions together: high impressions with low CTR usually points to snippet or intent-match issues, not ranking.

title: Google Search Central, Tell Google about localized versions of your page (hreflang)
text:
## What hreflang does
hreflang annotations tell Google about language and region variations of a page so Search can point users to the most appropriate version. They do not force which version ranks; Google still determines page language independently and hreflang is a signal, not a guarantee.

## Three implementation methods
All three are equivalent. HTML link elements in the head: <link rel="alternate" hreflang="en-GB" href="..." />. HTTP headers for non-HTML files: Link: <url>; rel="alternate"; hreflang="en-GB". XML sitemap using xhtml:link children inside each url entry.

## Code format
Use an ISO 639-1 language code (en, de, fr), optionally a hyphen and an ISO 3166-1 Alpha 2 region code (en-GB, de-CH). Script subtags are allowed (zh-Hans, zh-Hant). You cannot specify a region by itself. The reserved value x-default marks the fallback page for users whose language or region does not match any listed version, useful for a country or language selector.

## The reciprocal return-link rule
Each language version must list itself as well as all other versions. If page X links to page Y, page Y must link back to X, or the annotations may be ignored. Missing return links is the most common failure.

## Common mistakes
Using UK instead of the correct GB region code, specifying a country code by itself, omitting the self-referential link, and non-reciprocal (one-way) annotations. hreflang solves the wrong-language and duplicate near-identical language versions problem; it is not for pointing between different content.

title: Google Business Profile Help, Improve your local ranking on Google
text:
## The three local ranking factors
Google ranks local business results on three factors. Relevance is how well a Business Profile matches what someone is searching for; complete, detailed business information helps Google match the profile to relevant searches. Distance is how far each result is from the location term used in the search, or from the searcher's location if none is specified. Prominence is how well known a business is, based on information Google has about it from across the web (links, articles, directories) and also on Google review count and review score: more reviews and higher ratings improve local ranking.

## Best practices
Enter complete and accurate data: address, category, attributes, phone, and hours. Verify your locations so Google trusts they are authorized. Keep hours accurate, including holiday hours. Manage and respond to reviews, since interacting shows you value customers. Add high-quality photos. For retailers, list in-store products.

## What does not work
There is no way to request or pay for a better local ranking. Google does not disclose the algorithm and guards it to keep the ranking fair. Fake reviews, fake business locations, and keyword-stuffed business names violate the guidelines and can get a profile suspended.

title: Google Search Central Blog, Google Search's guidance about AI-generated content
text:
## Quality over production method
Google's approach to ranking has long rewarded high-quality content, however it is produced. Rather than focusing on how content is made, Google's systems focus on the quality of content. Using automation, including AI, to generate content with the primary purpose of manipulating ranking in search results is a violation of Google's spam policies.

## E-E-A-T still applies
Google rewards content that demonstrates Experience, Expertise, Authoritativeness, and Trustworthiness (E-E-A-T), regardless of how it was produced. Creators looking for success should produce original, high-quality, people-first content that shows E-E-A-T.

## Who, how, and why
When using AI, the same Who, How, and Why guidance applies. Who: make clear who authored the content. How: be transparent about how it was made, including where AI was involved, if that helps readers understand it (for example, AI assisted a data-heavy article). Where automation is used to generate the primary content, explaining that adds helpful context. Why: content should be created primarily to help people, not primarily to game search rankings, which is against the spam policies.

title: Google, Search Quality Rater Guidelines (General Guidelines), Sections 2 to 3.4
text:
## Purpose and beneficial purpose
The purpose of a page is the reason it was created. Every page is created for a purpose, and most are created to be helpful to people, giving the page a beneficial purpose. Some pages are created merely to make money with little effort to help people, and some are created to harm users. The goal of Page Quality (PQ) rating is to determine how well a page achieves its purpose. As long as a page is created to help people, no page type is inherently higher quality than another (encyclopedia pages are not necessarily higher quality than humor pages). If a page has a harmful purpose, or is designed to deceive people about its true purpose or who is responsible, it should be rated Lowest.

## YMYL (Your Money or Your Life)
YMYL topics can significantly impact the health, financial stability, or safety of people, or the welfare or well-being of society. Categories include YMYL Health or Safety, YMYL Financial Security, YMYL Government, Civics and Society (including election and voting information), and YMYL Other. A topic is YMYL when clear and present harm could result, or when inaccurate or untrustworthy content could cause harm, for example symptoms of a heart attack, how to invest money, what to do in an earthquake, or who can vote. Two test questions: would a careful person seek out experts or highly trusted sources to prevent harm, and is this a topic most people would be content to casually consult friends about. Pages on clear YMYL topics require the highest Page Quality standards.

## Main Content, Supplementary Content, Ads
Content on a page is classified as Main Content (MC), Supplementary Content (SC), or Advertisements/Monetization (Ads). MC is any part that directly helps the page achieve its purpose, including the page title. SC contributes to a good experience but does not directly help achieve the purpose, such as navigation links. Ads are content or links displayed for monetizing the page; the presence or absence of Ads is not by itself a reason for a High or Low rating. The quality of the MC plays a very large role in the PQ rating.

## Page Quality scale and quality of MC
The PQ sliding scale runs Lowest, Low, Medium, High, Highest, with in-between ratings (Lowest+, Low+, Medium+, High+). MC quality is judged by the effort, originality, and talent or skill that went into it, and for informational and YMYL pages, by accuracy and consistency with well-established expert consensus. Automatically generating thousands of pages with no oversight is not considered to have effort.

## Reputation research
Reputation research is required for all PQ tasks. Look for what independent, outside sources say about the website and content creator, not just what they say about themselves; when they disagree, trust the independent sources. Use searches that exclude the site's own pages (for example [ibm -site:ibm.com] and [ibm reviews -site:ibm.com]). For YMYL topics, reputation should be judged by what experts in the field say. A lack of reputation for small sites or ordinary people is neither positive nor negative.

## E-E-A-T with Trust at the center
Experience, Expertise, Authoritativeness, and Trust (E-E-A-T) are all important, and the most important member at the center of the family is Trust. Trust is the extent to which a page is accurate, honest, safe, and reliable. Experience is whether the creator has first-hand or life experience with the topic (for example a product review by someone who actually used the product). Expertise is the necessary knowledge or skill for the topic. Authoritativeness is being a known go-to source for the topic. Trust is most important because untrustworthy pages have low E-E-A-T no matter how experienced, expert, or authoritative they seem: a financial scam is untrustworthy even if run by an expert scammer. On clear YMYL topics that give information or advice, high expertise may be required to be trustworthy; but pages sharing genuine first-hand life experience on YMYL topics (for example coping with an illness) can have high E-E-A-T when the content is trustworthy, safe, and consistent with expert consensus.

title: Ahrefs Blog, What Is Search Intent? A Complete Guide
text:
## What search intent is
Search intent (also called keyword intent) is the reason behind a search query: what the searcher is actually looking for. Matching a page to intent is a prerequisite for ranking, because Google works hard to serve the result type that satisfies the query.

## The four main types
Informational intent: the searcher wants information or an answer to a question (for example how something works). Navigational intent: the searcher wants a specific website or page (a brand or login page). Commercial intent (commercial investigation): the searcher is researching or comparing before buying (for example best air fryer, product reviews). Transactional intent: the searcher is ready to act, usually to buy. A single keyword can carry multiple intents; best air fryer mixes informational, commercial, and transactional signals.

## The 3 Cs of search intent
To match intent, study the current top-ranking results along three dimensions. Content type: the dominant format ranking (blog post, video, product page, category page, landing page). Content format: the structure of the top pages (how-to, tutorial, listicle, review, comparison, opinion). Content angle: the dominant selling point or hook, such as recency (for example 2024) or a specific qualifier like for beginners.

## How to optimize
Look at what already ranks and align your page to those three Cs rather than fighting the SERP. If the results are all listicles and yours is a single product page, you have an intent mismatch and will struggle to rank. Also analyze common subtopics in the top pages to cover what searchers expect.

title: Backlinko (Brian Dean), Link Building for SEO: The Definitive Guide
text:
## What link building is and why it matters
Link building is the process of getting other websites to link back to your site to improve its authority and search rankings. Links act as a ranking signal, a discovery mechanism, and third-party validation of authority, and high-quality links reinforce E-E-A-T. Beyond followed backlinks, unlinked brand mentions and co-citations (your brand appearing alongside recognized authorities) also carry weight.

## What makes a good link
Prioritize links by authority and topical relevance: a link from a trusted, on-topic site matters most. Editorially earned links from established publications outweigh paid placements. Dofollow links pass more SEO value than nofollow, though nofollow still brings referral traffic and brand awareness. A natural link profile is diverse, and some lower-quality links mixed in is normal.

## White-hat strategies
Create linkable assets: original research and data, visual assets (charts, infographics), free tools, and comprehensive ultimate guides that become go-to references. Do prospecting by analyzing competitor backlink profiles and finding resource pages (for example site:.edu + topic + resources). Guest post on publications with real readership and editorial standards, focused on genuine value. Personalize outreach using the AIDA model (Attention, Interest, Desire, Action), keep pitches short (under 200 words), and follow up after 5 to 7 days. Named techniques include the Skyscraper approach (make a better version of a proven linkable asset then earn its links) and broken-link building.

## What to avoid (anti-patterns)
Buying links, link schemes and pure link exchanges, low-quality directories with exact-match spam anchors, Private Blog Networks (PBNs) built only to manipulate links, and unnatural patterns like sudden spikes in exact-match anchor text or links from unrelated domains. These violate Google's link spam policies.

title: Google Search Central, Block search indexing with noindex
text:
## What noindex does
The noindex rule tells search engines that support it to drop a page entirely from search results, regardless of whether other sites link to it. It is the correct tool to keep a page out of the index (unlike robots.txt, which only controls crawling).

## The critical robots.txt interaction
For noindex to work, the page must NOT be blocked by robots.txt. If the page is disallowed in robots.txt, Google cannot crawl it, never sees the noindex directive, and the page can still be indexed through external links. This is one of the most common technical SEO mistakes: combining Disallow in robots.txt with a noindex tag cancels the noindex.

## Implementation
Meta tag for all crawlers: <meta name="robots" content="noindex">. To target only Google: <meta name="googlebot" content="noindex">. For non-HTML resources (PDFs, images) use the HTTP header X-Robots-Tag: noindex. You can combine rules, for example <meta name="robots" content="noindex, nofollow">.

## Debugging
If a noindexed page still appears, Google usually has not recrawled since the change. Use the URL Inspection tool to request recrawling and confirm Googlebot can see the directive.

title: Google Search Central, Control your snippets in search results
text:
## How snippets are generated
Google automatically creates the snippet from the page's content to emphasize the parts most relevant to the user's query, so the same page can show different snippets for different searches. Google may use the meta description HTML element when it gives a more accurate description of the page than on-page text.

## Meta description best practices
Write a unique meta description for each page: identical or similar descriptions across a site are not helpful when individual pages appear in results. Make descriptions truly descriptive and accurate, and include relevant facts (author, date, price, manufacturer). Avoid strings of keywords. For large database-driven sites, programmatically generated descriptions are appropriate and encouraged, as long as they stay human-readable and diverse.

## Snippet controls
Use robots meta directives to control snippets: nosnippet prevents any snippet from showing; max-snippet:[number] limits snippet length to a number of characters; data-nosnippet is an HTML attribute that blocks a specific section of a page from appearing in a snippet. These give fine control without changing the page's indexing status.

title: Google Search Central, Google Search Essentials
text:
## The three parts
Google Search Essentials has three parts. Technical requirements: what Google needs from a page to show it, described as the bare minimum. Spam policies: behaviors and tactics that can lead to lower ranking or being omitted entirely. Key best practices: the things that can have the most impact on ranking and appearance.

## Technical requirements
There are very few technical things you must do. Googlebot must not be blocked (in robots.txt) from the page. The page must return a successful HTTP status code (a 200). The page must have indexable content in a supported format (not, for example, blocked or empty). Meeting these makes a page eligible to appear, but does not guarantee it.

## Key best practices
Create helpful, reliable, people-first content. Use words that people would use to look for your content, placed in prominent spots like the title and headings. Make your links crawlable so Google can find other pages on your site (use <a href> links with a resolvable URL). Tell people about your site and promote it in relevant communities. Follow the specific guidance for images, video, structured data, and JavaScript, and use features that improve how the site appears. Important caveat: meeting all requirements and best practices does not guarantee Google will crawl, index, or serve the page.

title: Ahrefs Blog, Internal Links for SEO: An Actionable Guide
text:
## What internal links do
Internal links connect pages within the same site. They help Google discover and crawl new pages, they pass PageRank (link equity) around the site so more-linked pages accumulate authority, they set topical context through descriptive anchor text, and they establish site architecture and hierarchy so Google understands how content relates.

## Types of internal links
Navigational links (menus), contextual links (editorial links inside the body), breadcrumb links, footer links, and related-content modules. Contextual links inside relevant body content carry the strongest topical signal.

## Best practices
Use a shallow, pyramid architecture keeping important pages within about three clicks of the home page, and reinforce it with topic clusters (a pillar page linking to and from related cluster pages). Add a few descriptive contextual links per article rather than stuffing dozens, which dilutes value and readability. Link from high-authority, high-traffic pages to the important pages you want to boost. Use varied, descriptive anchor text, not click here. Place important links high in the content.

## Anti-patterns to fix
Orphan pages have zero internal links, so Google struggles to find them and no authority flows to them; audit and link them. Fix internal links pointing to 404s, which waste authority. Keep important links dofollow and crawlable across devices. Over-linking with exact-match anchors everywhere looks manipulative and spreads PageRank too thin.

title: Schema.org, Getting Started with Schema.org using Microdata
text:
## What schema.org is
Schema.org is a collaborative, shared vocabulary founded by Google, Microsoft, Yahoo, and Yandex that webmasters use to add machine-readable meaning to web content. Search engines have a limited understanding of what a page discusses; schema.org markup bridges that gap so engines can understand entities and their properties.

## The three core attributes (Microdata)
itemscope marks a section of the page as describing a specific item. itemtype specifies the item's type using a schema.org URL, for example https://schema.org/Movie. itemprop labels a property of that item, for example itemprop="director" or itemprop="name". Items can be embedded: a director property can itself be a Person item with its own name and birthDate properties.

## The type hierarchy
Schema.org uses inheritance. The broadest type is Thing, which has four properties: name, description, url, and image. More specific types inherit from broader ones. Common types include creative works (Book, Movie, Recipe), Event, Organization, Person, Place, Product, and Review.

## Machine-readable disambiguation
To express data unambiguously: use <time datetime="YYYY-MM-DD"> for dates and times, <link href> to point to enumerated allowed values, and <meta content> to supply data that is not otherwise visible on the page. JSON-LD is an alternative and Google-preferred syntax, but the itemscope/itemtype/itemprop model is the same vocabulary.

title: Google Search Central, A guide to Google Search ranking systems
text:
## Systems vs updates
Google distinguishes ongoing ranking systems (persistent technologies built into core ranking) from ranking updates (specific, announced changes tracked on the status dashboard). Ranking happens primarily at the page level: Google uses a variety of signals and systems to rank individual pages.

## The helpful content system moved into core ranking
The helpful content system, first announced in 2022, became part of Google's core ranking systems in March 2024, so the line between a discrete update and a foundational system has blurred for that mechanism. The people-first, helpful, reliable content guidance is therefore now expressed through core updates rather than a standalone system.

## Named ongoing systems
RankBrain, an AI system that helps Google understand how words relate to concepts and match queries. Passage ranking, which identifies individual sections of a page to assess relevance. The reviews system, which rewards high-quality, in-depth reviews with original research and first-hand expertise over thin summaries. Deduplication systems that avoid showing unhelpful duplicate results. The exact match domain system, which stops a domain that merely matches the query words from getting undue credit. Site diversity, which generally avoids showing more than two listings from the same site for a query. Crisis information and other systems address specific needs. These systems work together to surface relevant, reliable content and filter spam.
